issues.addMap: Add the map that will be used to stratify the sample.
issues.chooseCrs: Choose the equal-area projection areas are computed in.
issues.countPixels: Count the map’s pixels in the reporting area.
issues.nameValues: Name every map class so the strata can be defined.
issues.twoClasses: Define at least two reporting classes; one class cannot be estimated alone.
issues.emptyClass: Every reporting class needs at least one map class assigned to it.
issues.unassigned: Assign every map class to a stratum, or mark it as nodata.
issues.chooseTarget: Choose the target class the sample size is solved for.
issues.precisionRange: Target precision must be between 0 and 100 percent.
issues.noUnits: The design has no sampling units; check the pixel counts and the target class.

panel.incomplete: The sample is incomplete. These figures are already unbiased, but their confidence intervals will keep narrowing, and any unit still unannotated could move them. Do not publish them yet.

reading.title: Reading these numbers
reading.technical1: Areas come from the stratified estimator: p̂<sub>k</sub> = Σ W<sub>i</sub>(n<sub>ik</sub>/n<sub>i</sub>), with the standard error of Olofsson Eq. 10 and a 95% interval of ±1.96 standard errors. The map column is the pixel-counting figure and is shown only so the size of the map's bias is visible.
reading.technical2: UA is user's accuracy (Eq. 1, variance Eq. 6); PA is producer's accuracy (Eq. 3, variance Eq. 7). They answer different questions and are rarely equal: a class the map over-calls scores low on the first and high on the second.
reading.body: Each row is what the annotated units say the area really is, with the range it could plausibly be. Where the map column sits outside that range, the map was systematically over- or under-calling that class. UA (user's accuracy) is how much of what the map called this class really was it; PA(producer's accuracy) is how much of what really was this class the map caught.

columns.uaTitle: User's accuracy: of what the map calls this class, how much really is it
columns.paTitle: Producer's accuracy: of what really is this class, how much the map found

panel.overall: Overall map accuracy {{accuracy}} ± {{margin}}, from {{units}} annotated sampling units.

setup.activated: The sample design is set. The sampling units will be drawn next.
setup.saveFailed: Could not save the sample design
setup.title: Sample design
setup.pilotRunning: A pilot is running. The full design is proposed once its units are annotated.
setup.lockedNote: The sample lives in {{name}}, and that set is managed by this design: tasks cannot be added to it, imported into it or moved into it by hand. Every unit in it has a known inclusion probability; a task added by hand has none, and one such task is enough to make the estimate indefensible.

data.areasFailed: Could not read the area file
data.countFailed: Could not count the map pixels
data.title: Map & Areas of Interest
data.technical1: Counting the pixels of a class and calling that its area is a biased estimator: a classifier that confuses two classes moves area between them, and no amount of extra pixels corrects it. The map is used only as a stratification variable, so its errors cost precision rather than accuracy.
data.technical2: Pixel counts enter the design as stratum weights W<sub>i</sub>, and appear in the results only as a contrast to the sample-based estimate.
data.source: Olofsson et al. (2014), Good practices for estimating area and assessing accuracy of land change, Sections 2.1.1 and 4.4.
data.intro: The map you upload divides the reporting area into strata, so that the sample spends most of its units where they matter. The area figures you publish come from what annotators see at the sampling units, not from the map. That is what makes the result unbiased even when the map itself is imperfect.
data.mapIntro: A classified raster: one integer per pixel giving the predicted class.
data.uploadFileHint: A GeoTIFF from your own machine.
data.linkMapHint: A cloud-optimized GeoTIFF already on the web.
data.requirementInteger: One integer value per class. Continuous probability rasters cannot be used as strata.
data.requirementCoverage: Covering all of the areas you want to report on.
data.bandHint: Which band of the file holds the classification.
data.crsProposed: Areas are computed in a Lambert azimuthal equal-area projection centred on this map. It preserves area everywhere, which is the only property pixel counts depend on, so there is nothing to choose here unless your office publishes in a particular projection.
data.crsHint: Pixel counts only stand for area on an equal-area grid, so they are reprojected into this one before they become stratum weights. Any PROJ string or EPSG code is accepted.
data.useProposedCrs: Use the projection proposed for this map.
data.notEqualArea: This projection does not preserve area, so pixel counts taken in it are not proportional to ground area and the stratum weights would be wrong.
data.namesIntro: Every distinct value in the band, and the class it stands for. Which of them are nodata is settled on the next step.
data.noLegend: This band carries no class list, so the distinct values have to be read from the pixels and named by hand.
data.missingNames_one: {{count}} value still need a name. The file did not carry class names, so they have to be typed in.
data.missingNames_other: {{count}} values still need a name. The file did not carry class names, so they have to be typed in.
data.areasIntro: Leave this empty and the whole of the map is the reporting area: one sample, one set of figures, covering everything the raster spans. Add boundaries when the estimate has to stop at one, or be reported region by region. Upload a file of oblasts, for example, and each feature becomes an area you can report on; a feature made of several separate pieces is still one area.
data.counting: Counting map pixels in the reporting area…
data.pixelsCountedWholeMap: {{pixels}} pixels in the reporting area, which is the whole map
data.domainTitle: How should these areas be reported?
data.combined: One number for all areas together
data.combinedHint: Cheapest. You get a national figure with the precision you ask for. Per-area numbers can still be produced afterwards, but they will be much less precise.
data.perArea: A separate number for each area
data.perAreaHint: Each area gets its own sample and reaches the requested precision on its own. Expect the total sample size to multiply by the number of areas.

classes.nodataTechnical: Excluding nodata removes it from the target population: the stratum weights are renormalised over what remains and the reported total area shrinks accordingly. Keeping it as a stratum leaves it in the population and allows sampling units inside it to carry a real reference label, which is what recovers area the map failed to assign. Nodata is never a reporting class either way.
classes.nodataIntro: Nodata pixels are not a class you report on, but they are still ground. The choice defines the target population, and therefore what your published total covers.
classes.exclude: Exclude them from the target population
classes.excludeHint: Correct when the nodata pixels lie outside what you report on: sea, another country, permanent cloud. Your published total then covers the mapped part only.
classes.keep: Keep them as their own stratum
classes.keepHint: Correct when they are land inside your reporting area that the map simply failed on. Sampling units fall there too, so crop the map missed still enters your total.
classes.title: Reporting classes and strata
classes.technical1: Each reporting class becomes one stratum. Aggregating map classes before sampling is usually preferable to reporting them separately and summing afterwards: a merged stratum carries a single sample size that can be driven to the precision required, whereas thin strata each need their own minimum.
classes.technical2: Aggregation introduces no bias. The reference labels are recorded against this same class list, so the estimated error matrix stays square and the stratum weights continue to sum to one.
classes.source: Olofsson et al. (2014), Section 2.1.1 on aggregating map classes into strata.
classes.intro: The classes you publish need not be the classes the map produced. If the map separates wheat, barley and rye but you report a single winter cereals figure, assign all three to one reporting class here. Each reporting class becomes one stratum of the sample design, so fewer and larger classes reach a given precision with a smaller sample.
classes.defineTechnical1: An annotator looking at the imagery available at a sampling unit has to be able to decide reliably whether that unit is the class. This is a requirement of the response design rather than a preference.
classes.defineTechnical2: The estimator treats the reference classification as correct, so error in it is not averaged away by a larger sample: it propagates directly into the estimated area and the estimated accuracies. It is the one error a probability sample cannot correct for.
classes.defineTechnical3: Where two classes cannot be separated on screen, merge them in step 2 and report the combined class. A coarser class annotators can apply consistently is worth more than a finer one they cannot.
classes.defineSource: Olofsson et al. (2014), Section 3 on the response design.
classes.defineIntro: The rows of your published table. Each one becomes a stratum of the sample design, and each is a label an annotator will be asked to assign at a sampling unit. Every class must therefore be photointerpretable.
classes.assignIntro: Every class the map produces has to be accounted for. Two or more map classes assigned to the same reporting class are merged into a single stratum.
classes.nodataExcluded: Pixels marked nodata are excluded from the sample and from the area you publish: no sampling unit falls on them.
classes.nodataKept: Pixels marked nodata are kept as their own stratum, so sampling units fall on them too and ground the map failed to classify still enters your published total.
classes.unassignedWarning_one: {{count}} map class is not assigned yet. Every pixel of the reporting area has to fall in exactly one stratum, otherwise the stratum weights do not sum to the area you are reporting on.
classes.unassignedWarning_other: {{count}} map classes are not assigned yet. Every pixel of the reporting area has to fall in exactly one stratum, otherwise the stratum weights do not sum to the area you are reporting on.

prior.title: What is already known about this map?
prior.technical1: Sample size planning requires a conjectured error matrix. The stratum standard deviations S<sub>i</sub> = √(UA<sub>i</sub>(1 − UA<sub>i</sub>)) are derived from the conjectured user's accuracies, and those standard deviations are what Neyman allocation divides the sample size by. A mis-specified conjecture changes only the allocation, and an ineffective allocation of sample size to strata does not bias the estimators of area or accuracy.
prior.technical2: This is also why the design may be revised mid-campaign: stratified random sampling accommodates a change of sample size after collection has begun, provided the strata themselves stay fixed.
prior.intro: Allocating the sample across strata requires a conjecture about how accurate the map is. The conjecture is used only to decide how many sampling units each stratum receives. It does not enter the estimator, so an optimistic or pessimistic conjecture widens or narrows your confidence interval but cannot bias the area you publish.
prior.knowingTitle: What counts as knowing how accurate a map is
prior.knowingTechnical: The error matrix is estimated in units of area proportion, p̂<sub>ij</sub> = W<sub>i</sub>(n<sub>ij</sub>/n<sub>i</sub>), not as raw sample counts. This is what makes the accuracy measures and the area estimates consistent with each other, and it is why the stratum weights W<sub>i</sub> have to come from a full pixel count rather than from the sample.
prior.knowingSource: Olofsson et al. (2014), Sections 2.2, 4.1 and 4.2; Stehman and Foody (2019), Key issues in rigorous accuracy assessment.
prior.knowingIntro: An accuracy figure is not a property of a classifier. It is an estimate of a population quantity, obtained from a probability sample of the mapped area whose units carry a reference classification of higher quality than the map. That sample yields an error matrix, and the three familiar measures are read off it.
prior.uaDefinition: Of the area the map assigns to a class, the proportion that really is that class. Its complement is commission error - what the map over-called.
prior.paDefinition: Of the area that really is a class, the proportion the map assigned to it. Its complement is omission error - what the map missed.
prior.oaDefinition: The proportion of the whole mapped area the map classifies correctly. It is dominated by the largest classes, so it says little about a rare crop.
prior.notCounting: Three things do not count, however carefully they were produced: accuracy measured on training data, accuracy from a convenience or purposive sample, and a per-class figure resting on a handful of units. Each describes the units that happened to be labelled rather than the mapped population, and none carries a defensible confidence interval.
prior.basisTitle: What is the conjecture based on?
prior.basisIntro: The stronger the basis, the closer the allocation lands to optimal. Every option here produces a valid estimate; they differ in how efficiently the sample is spent.

last_season_map.title: An accuracy assessment of last season of this same map
last_season_map.summary: This map was produced before and assessed against reference data.
last_season_map.rationale: The same method over the same landscape tends to make the same kinds of error, so last season’s estimated user’s accuracies are the best available conjecture for this season. If that assessment used a probability sample of the map, its accuracies describe the whole mapped population and carry over directly.

published_map.title: A published accuracy assessment of a comparable map
published_map.summary: Another producer mapped this region and published assessed accuracies.
published_map.rationale: The landscape is right but the classifier is not yours, so the accuracies transfer only approximately. Check that the published figures come from a probability sample, and that the class definitions match yours: per-class accuracies are comparable only when the classes are.

expert_judgement.title: Expert judgement
expert_judgement.summary: Analysts familiar with this map and this region conjecture its accuracy.
expert_judgement.rationale: Acceptable when the experts have actually inspected this map’s output. It is a conjecture rather than an estimate, so keep the per-stratum minimum in place and expect to revise the allocation once reference labels start arriving.

held_out_test_set.title: A held-out test set from the map’s own development
held_out_test_set.summary: Labelled units set aside while the classifier was trained.
held_out_test_set.rationale: Admissible here, and only here, because these conjectures are used solely to allocate the sample across strata. Allocation affects precision, never bias, so an optimistic conjecture cannot corrupt the published area. Two pitfalls make the same numbers inadmissible anywhere else. First, a test set is almost never a probability sample of the mapped population: it sits where reference data was convenient to collect, so accuracies computed from it have unknown inclusion probabilities and are typically optimistic by a wide margin. Second, it comes from the map’s own development, so it lets the classifier grade itself. Treat the values below as an upper bound, consider entering figures several points lower, and do not publish accuracies from this source - the assessment this campaign produces is the one you report.

none.title: No usable accuracy information
none.summary: This map has never been assessed against reference data.
none.rationale: A pilot measures the accuracies instead of conjecturing them. Pilot units are drawn from the same strata by the same protocol, so they remain part of the final sample and enter the estimator with the same weights; nothing is discarded.

prior.uaTitle: Conjectured user's accuracy of each stratum
prior.uaTechnical: Producer's accuracy cannot be substituted here. PA is a ratio whose denominator runs across every stratum, so it is not a property of the stratum being sized and is not knowable until the reference labels are in. UA is a within-stratum proportion, which is exactly what the stratum standard deviation needs.
prior.uaSource: Olofsson et al. (2014), Section 5.1.1 and Table 6.
prior.uaIntro: For each stratum: of every 100 pixels the map assigns to it, how many really are that class. Both UA and PA are estimated from the finished sample and published beside the area; only UA has to be conjectured in advance.
prior.startingValues: Starting values come from {{source}}. Revise any stratum you have better information about and leave the rest as they are.
prior.pilotTechnical: The pilot is the first phase of a two-phase design. Its units are drawn from the same strata by the same protocol, so they remain part of the final stratified sample and enter the estimator with the same weights. Only the allocation of the remaining sample size is chosen using them, and the choice of allocation does not affect unbiasedness.
prior.pilotIntro: The next step plans a pilot rather than a full design. Once the pilot units are annotated, this page estimates the map's accuracies from them and proposes the full sample from measured figures instead of conjectured ones. Pilot units are retained and count towards the final sample size.

neyman.name: Optimal for the target class
neyman.description: Concentrates the sample where the target class is most uncertain, giving the smallest confidence interval for it at a given sample size.
neyman.theory: Neyman allocation: n_i proportional to W_i·S_i, the stratum weight times the stratum standard deviation. It is the exact minimiser of the target class variance for a fixed total sample size, so no other rule beats it on that one estimate - and it is why a stratum the map gets almost always right receives few units while a mixed stratum receives many.

proportional.name: Proportional to stratum weight
proportional.description: Best for overall accuracy and for the largest strata, at the cost of the rare ones.
proportional.theory: Proportional allocation: n_i proportional to W_i alone. Every sampling unit then carries the same weight, which makes the estimator self-weighting and minimises the variance of overall accuracy. Rare strata receive almost nothing, which is what the per-stratum minimum exists to correct.

equal.name: Equal across strata
equal.description: Best when the accuracy of each individual class matters more than any area figure. Inefficient for area estimation.
equal.theory: Equal allocation: n_i = n/k. It equalises the precision of each stratum's user's accuracy, which is why accuracy assessments favour it, but it heavily over-samples small strata for area estimation, where a stratum's contribution to the total is weighted by W_i.

official.title: Official national statistics
official.example: What USDA’s National Agricultural Statistics Service targets for maize, soybean and winter wheat area. Expensive: it needs thousands of sampling units.

national.title: National reporting, main crops
national.example: Good enough to publish a national planted area and to detect a real year-on-year change. The usual choice for a ministry’s headline crop.

monitoring.title: Programme monitoring
monitoring.example: Enough to track a trend, size a subsidy programme, or report a minor crop. A 1.0 Mha estimate would carry roughly ±0.2 Mha.

design.floorRationale: A stratum with a small weight receives almost no sampling units under proportional allocation, and a handful of units cannot support a statement about that class. Olofsson et al. (2014) recommend 50 to 100 units in each rare stratum. Raising the floor widens the intervals of the other strata only if units are taken away from them, which this tool does not do: it adds to the total sample size instead.
design.pilotTechnical: A flat budget per stratum with a proportional split gives every stratum enough units to estimate its own user's accuracy to within roughly ±0.07 at 50 units, which is enough to drive the Neyman allocation of the remaining sample size. The pilot units remain part of the final stratified sample.
design.pilotIntro: Without a usable accuracy estimate, the campaign starts by measuring the map rather than guessing at it. These units are annotated first; once they are done, this page recomputes the full design from the accuracies the pilot measured, and the units already annotated count towards it.
design.budgetHint: What the pilot buys per class, then spread by how much of the map each covers.
design.floorHint: No class falls below this, however little of the map it covers.
design.title: Sample design
design.technical: Expected precision is √(Σ W<sub>i</sub>² S<sub>i</sub>² / n<sub>i</sub>) divided by the expected proportion, the design-stage form of the stratified standard error. It is an anticipation under the assumed error matrix, not a guarantee: the interval you finally publish is computed from the annotated sampling units.
design.source: Olofsson et al. (2014), Eq. 10 and Table 7.
design.intro: The sample size, and how it is allocated across the strata. Every figure here is editable. The precision shown is what this design is expected to deliver under the conjectured accuracies of the previous step; the interval you publish is computed from the annotated sampling units and appears on the campaign overview as work progresses.
design.targetTechnical: Allocation trades precision between strata. Neyman allocation minimises the variance of one estimator, so the objective has to be named before the sample sizes can be solved. Choosing a different target later only changes the allocation, never the validity of units already collected.
design.targetIntro: The class whose area drives the sample size. Every other class is still estimated, and you will see the precision each of them reaches. Choose the crop your office publishes and has to defend, usually the one with the greatest policy or market consequence. A rare class is expensive to pin down: making a 2% class the target costs far more units than a 30% class.
design.precisionTechnical: The target is a coefficient of variation: the standard error of the estimated proportion divided by the proportion itself. Sample size follows from Cochran's stratified formula with the target standard error set to CV × p̂. A 95% confidence interval is roughly ±1.96 × CV of the estimate.
design.precisionIntro: How much uncertainty you are willing to publish alongside the number, stated as a percentage of the number itself. At 5%, an estimate of 1.00 Mha comes with a 95% confidence interval of roughly ±0.10 Mha. Tighter targets are costly: halving the interval requires roughly four times the sample size.
design.customAria: Target precision, percent of the estimate
design.customHint: percent of the estimate. Below 2% the sample size grows very quickly.
design.overridden: Some sample sizes were edited by hand. The expected precision below reflects your numbers, not the computed ones.
design.allocationTitle: How the sample size is allocated across strata
design.allocationTechnical: With n<sub>i</sub> = a<sub>i</sub>n, the variance of the stratified estimator is (1/n)·Σ(W<sub>i</sub>²S<sub>i</sub>²/a<sub>i</sub>), so the rule is the choice of the shares a<sub>i</sub>. Minimising that expression over the shares gives Neyman; setting a<sub>i</sub> = W<sub>i</sub> gives proportional; a<sub>i</sub> = 1/k gives equal. All three are design-unbiased, and an ineffective allocation costs precision rather than correctness.
design.allocationSource: Cochran (1977), Eqs. 5.25 and 5.26; Olofsson et al. (2014), Section 5.1.2.
design.allocationIntro: All three are design-unbiased. They differ only in which estimate ends up most precise.

curve.aria: Expected confidence interval against sample size for {{n}} classes
